title: Scaling and Managing Model Services on Kubernetes
summary: Learn how to run model serving workloads reliably on Kubernetes by configuring resource requests/limits, autoscaling with HPA, and safe rolling updates with health probes.
objectives: Set appropriate CPU/memory requests and limits for model serving pods
Configure Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) to scale model services under load
Perform safe rolling updates and rollbacks with zero downtime
Use liveness, readiness, and startup probes to keep traffic flowing to healthy pods
Apply PodDisruptionBudgets and node strategies to maintain availability

quiz.q: What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit?
options: It is removed from Service endpoints
quiz.why: Exceeding a memory limit triggers an OOMKill, unlike CPU which is throttled. This is why memory request should be close to the limit for model servers.

quiz.q: Which probe is most important for a model with a slow weight-loading startup?
quiz.why: The startupProbe gives slow-starting containers time to initialize before liveness and readiness probes begin, preventing premature restarts.

quiz.q: Why is CPU utilization often a poor scaling metric for inference services?
options: CPU is never used by models
Request rate or queue depth better reflects real inference load
CPU metrics are not available in Kubernetes
quiz.why: Inference load correlates better with requests-per-second or queue depth than raw CPU, so custom metrics via Prometheus Adapter or KEDA scale more accurately.

quiz.q: What does setting maxUnavailable: 0 in a rolling update achieve?
options: Faster rollout by killing all pods at once
Full serving capacity is maintained throughout the rollout
quiz.why: maxUnavailable: 0 ensures no existing pods are removed until replacements are Ready, keeping full capacity during the update (requires surge room).

quiz.q: What is the role of a PodDisruptionBudget?
quiz.answer: It guarantees a minimum number of healthy pods remain available during voluntary disruptions such as node drains or cluster upgrades.
quiz.why: PDBs protect availability against voluntary disruptions, ensuring operations like node maintenance don't take down too many model serving pods at once.

quiz.q: Which two Kubernetes components must work together so HPA scale-ups can actually run?
quiz.answer: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (which adds pods) and the Cluster Autoscaler (which adds nodes for those pods to land on).
quiz.why: HPA only creates pods; if no node has capacity they stay Pending, so the Cluster Autoscaler must add nodes to realize the scale-up.

resources.label: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

body_markdown:
## Why Kubernetes for Model Serving

Model services have unique traffic patterns: bursty inference loads, slow cold starts (loading large weights), and strict latency SLOs. Kubernetes gives us declarative scaling, self-healing, and rolling updates—but only if we configure resources, autoscaling, and health checks correctly.

## Resource Requests and Limits

Every container should declare `requests` (what the scheduler reserves) and `limits` (the hard ceiling).

- **requests** drive scheduling and HPA utilization math.
- **limits** prevent a noisy pod from starving neighbors. CPU over-limit is throttled; memory over-limit triggers an OOMKill.
- For model servers, profile real inference memory (weights + batch activations) and set memory request ≈ limit to avoid OOM surprises. Avoid setting a CPU limit far below request, or you'll throttle latency.

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: "4Gi"
  limits:
    cpu: "2"
    memory: "4Gi"
```

For GPU models, request `nvidia.com/gpu: 1`; GPUs are not oversubscribed, so request == limit always.

## Health Probes

Three probe types keep traffic on healthy pods:

- **startupProbe**: gives slow-loading models time to load weights before other probes start. Critical for large models.
- **readinessProbe**: pod only receives traffic when ready; failing it removes the pod from the Service endpoints without killing it.
- **livenessProbe**: restarts a hung pod.

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
```

## Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)

HPA adds/removes replicas based on metrics. CPU is the default, but for inference, custom metrics like requests-per-second or queue depth (via Prometheus Adapter / KEDA) are far better proxies for load.

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: model-hpa }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: model-server
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 }
```

Tune `behavior` to avoid flapping: scale up fast, scale down slowly with stabilization windows. HPA needs metrics-server installed and accurate `requests` to compute utilization.

## Rolling Updates and Rollbacks

Deployments default to `RollingUpdate`. Control disruption with `maxUnavailable` and `maxSurge`.

```yaml
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxUnavailable: 0
    maxSurge: 1
```

- `maxUnavailable: 0` ensures full capacity during rollout (needs spare node room).
- Readiness probes gate the rollout—new pods must be Ready before old ones terminate.
- Roll back with `kubectl rollout undo deployment/model-server`.
- Use `minReadySeconds` to bake new pods before considering them stable.

## Availability: PDBs and Disruptions

A **PodDisruptionBudget** protects against voluntary disruptions (node drains, upgrades) by guaranteeing a minimum of healthy pods.

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: model-server }
```

Combine with `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` and a `preStop` hook so in-flight requests drain before shutdown.

## Putting It Together

A production-ready model service: 2+ minReplicas, profiled requests/limits, startup+readiness+liveness probes, HPA on a meaningful metric, zero-downtime rolling strategy, and a PDB. Add a Cluster Autoscaler so HPA scale-ups can actually land on new nodes.

slides.title: Scaling and Managing Model Services on Kubernetes
slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll make a model serving workload reliable under real production load on Kubernetes. We'll cover resource limits, health probes, autoscaling, rolling updates, and disruption budgets — the practical knobs an MLOps engineer turns every day.

slides.title: Why Model Serving Is Different
bullets: Slow cold starts loading large model weights
Often memory- or GPU-bound, not just CPU
slides.narration: Model services aren't typical web apps. Traffic is bursty, weights take time to load so cold starts are slow, and you usually have tight latency targets. They're frequently memory or GPU bound. Kubernetes can handle this well, but only if we configure scheduling, scaling, and health checks deliberately.

slides.title: Resource Requests and Limits
bullets: requests = reserved for scheduling and HPA math
limits = hard ceiling; CPU throttles, memory OOMKills
Set memory request ≈ limit to avoid OOM surprises
slides.narration: Requests are what the scheduler reserves and what HPA uses to compute utilization. Limits are hard ceilings: exceed CPU and you get throttled, exceed memory and the pod is OOM killed. For model servers, profile real memory usage and keep the memory request close to the limit. GPUs are never oversubscribed, so request always equals limit.

slides.title: Health Probes
bullets: readinessProbe: gates traffic without killing the pod
Wrong probes cause flapping or dropped requests
slides.code:
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
slides.narration: Three probes work together. The startup probe gives a large model time to load before other probes run. The readiness probe controls whether a pod receives traffic — failing it removes the pod from the Service without killing it. The liveness probe restarts a truly hung container. Misconfigured probes are a top cause of dropped requests, so tune the timings to your load time.

slides.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
bullets: Scales replicas on CPU or custom metrics
RPS or queue depth beats CPU for inference
slides.code:
minReplicas: 2
maxReplicas: 20
metrics:
- type: Resource
  resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } }
slides.narration: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds and removes replicas based on metrics. CPU utilization is the default, but for inference, custom metrics like requests-per-second or queue depth — exposed through Prometheus Adapter or KEDA — track real load much better. HPA needs metrics-server and accurate resource requests to do its math. Use the behavior block to scale up quickly but scale down slowly so you don't flap.

slides.title: Rolling Updates and Rollbacks
bullets: kubectl rollout undo for instant rollback
slides.narration: Deployments roll out new versions gradually. maxSurge and maxUnavailable control how aggressive that is. Setting maxUnavailable to zero keeps full capacity during the rollout, assuming you have node room for the surge. Readiness probes gate each step — new pods must be Ready before old ones go. If something breaks, kubectl rollout undo gets you back to the previous version fast.

slides.title: Availability During Disruptions
bullets: minAvailable keeps pods up during node drains
preStop hook + grace period drains in-flight requests
Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes for HPA scale-ups
slides.code:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: model-server } }
slides.narration: Node upgrades and drains are voluntary disruptions. A PodDisruptionBudget guarantees a minimum number of healthy pods stay up through them. Pair it with a preStop hook and a sensible termination grace period so in-flight inference requests drain cleanly. And remember: HPA can only scale up if nodes exist, so run the Cluster Autoscaler to add capacity on demand.

slides.title: Production Checklist
bullets: HPA on a meaningful metric with anti-flap behavior
slides.narration: Putting it together, a production-ready model service runs at least two replicas with profiled resources, has all three probe types configured, autoscales on a metric that reflects real load, rolls out without downtime, and is protected by a disruption budget. Add the Cluster Autoscaler underneath and your serving layer can survive both traffic spikes and cluster maintenance.
